outcome: No characterisation of the word-representable planar graphs has appeared since 26 January 2024. The one new planar-type characterisation, arXiv:2605.25733 (posted 25 May 2026), covers word-representable near-triangulations, a proper subclass of planar graphs, and its authors state that word-representability of planar graphs remains open.
problem_asks: (1) Characterise the word-representable planar graphs: give a description that decides, for any planar graph, whether it admits a word representation (a word over its vertices in which two letters alternate exactly when they are adjacent; equivalently, a semi-transitive orientation). (2) The '(non-)' in the title also asks for the complementary class, the non-word-representable planar graphs, to be characterised; this is the same question seen from the other side. The statement does not fix the form a characterisation must take (a structural description, a forbidden induced subgraph list, or something else), so a full answer would decide every planar graph. It asks about all planar graphs, not a subclass such as triangulations or near-triangulations. It does not ask about word-representable near-triangulations containing K4, which the Kitaev and Lozin survey lists as a separate item.

events.what_happened: Suchanda Roy and Ramesh Hariharasubramanian (IIT Guwahati), arXiv:2605.25733, 'Characterization of Word-Representable Near-Triangulations'. A near-triangulation is a planar graph in which every face except the outer face is a triangle. The paper claims a complete characterisation of word-representable near-triangulations by forbidden induced subgraphs. Theorem 16 (per the HTML text I read, summarised by a small model): a near-triangulation with outer face of any length, with or without K4, is word-representable iff it contains none of the graphs in Figure 8 (labelled A, A′, A″, A‴, B, B′, B″, C, C′, D, E, F, G, H, F1, F2, F3) and no odd wheel W2k+1 with k>1 as an induced subgraph. Theorem 15: a K4-free near-triangulation is word-representable iff it contains no induced odd wheel. The authors say the result unifies and extends the earlier characterisations for polyomino triangulations, triangulations of rectangular polyominoes with a single domino tile, K4-free near-triangulations, face subdivisions of triangular grid graphs, triangulations of grid-covered cylinder graphs, and chordal near-triangulations. They also say they correct inaccuracies in earlier work: they rectify a result of Glen (2016) stated as 'a K4-free near-triangulation is word-representable iff it is perfect', and they correct Kitaev and Sun (2024) by identifying a minimal non-word-representable graph on seven vertices that is not among the 25 listed there. Their introduction states that word-representability of planar graphs 'remains one of the most challenging problems in this area'.
events.revisions: Single version, v1, posted 25 May 2026 (arXiv listing). No later version found.
events.delivers: A forbidden-induced-subgraph characterisation of word-representability for near-triangulations, per the authors, including those containing K4. Restricted to near-triangulations: every inner face must be a triangle. It does not cover planar graphs that have a non-triangular inner face.
events.remains: Word-representability of every planar graph that is not a near-triangulation, that is, planar graphs with at least one inner face that is not a triangle. The authors say the general planar problem remains open. The paper's result also covers the sibling item (near-triangulations containing K4), which is not this statement.
events.time_since_posted: About 4.5 months at 11 October 2026. My searches found no review, comment, erratum, citing paper or journal version. I did not read the arXiv comments field.
events.directly_checkable: The forbidden graphs (the Figure 8 family and the odd wheels) are finite, so for a given near-triangulation the criterion reduces to a finite induced-subgraph test. The seven-vertex graph could be checked by a semi-transitive orientation search, as in the Kitaev and Sun method. I have not checked either myself.
events.doubts: (1) Single 2026 arXiv version; no journal acceptance found. (2) The paper corrects two earlier published results, Glen (2016) and Kitaev and Sun (2024). For Glen, the Roy paper states the result as 'word-representable iff perfect'; Glen's own abstract and the search results I read state it as 'iff 3-colourable'. Which is Glen's actual claim is not resolved by what I read (see disputes). (3) The PDF text could not be extracted with my tools, so the theorem statements above come from an HTML fetch that a small model summarised. I did not read the proofs, the Figure 8 graphs, or the seven-vertex graph, so the statements are summaries and not verbatim quotations.
events.direction: Toward a characterisation, but only for near-triangulations. It gives a complete forbidden-subgraph criterion for that class, including non-word-representable members (the odd wheels, which are planar, and the Figure 8 family). It does not decide word-representability for planar graphs outside the class, so for the bullet as stated it is a restricted-class result, neither a resolution nor a refutation.
events.object: Per the authors (HTML text, summarised): the forbidden induced subgraphs are the Figure 8 family (A, A′, A″, A‴, B, B′, B″, C, C′, D, E, F, G, H, F1, F2, F3) and the odd wheels W2k+1 for k>1; a near-triangulation is word-representable iff it contains none of them. The paper also exhibits a minimal non-word-representable graph on seven vertices that is not among Kitaev and Sun's list of 25. I did not read its construction and did not establish whether it is planar. The individual Figure 8 graphs and their proofs were not read.

events.what_happened: Marc Elliot Glen, 'Colourability and word-representability of near-triangulations', arXiv:1605.01688. Shows that a K4-free near-triangulation is word-representable iff it is 3-colourable, equivalently internally even, with a much shorter proof of the colourability fact. Says that it solves all open problems stated in an earlier paper it cites (the abstract identifies it only as reference [5]; I did not identify it).

events.delivers: For K4-free near-triangulations only: word-representable iff 3-colourable.
events.remains: Word-representability of near-triangulations that contain K4, and of all planar graphs outside the near-triangulation class.

events.what_happened: Thomas Z.Q. Chen, Sergey Kitaev and Brian Y. Sun, 'Word-representability of triangulations of grid-covered cylinder graphs', arXiv:1507.06749. Shows that for triangulations of grid-covered cylinder graphs, word-representability with three sectors is characterised by avoiding a set of six minimal induced subgraphs, and with more than three sectors by avoiding the wheels W5 and W7. Notes that the 3-colourability criterion fails for this class, since some word-representable members have chromatic number 4. Published in Discrete Applied Mathematics 213 (2016) 60–70, per a search snippet.

events.delivers: Triangulations of grid-covered cylinder graphs, split by number of sectors: a forbidden-subgraph characterisation (six minimal induced subgraphs for three sectors; W5 and W7 for more than three). Restricted to that class. The abstract does not state planarity explicitly; the cylinder grid embeds in an annulus, so the class appears to be planar, but I did not confirm this from the text.
events.remains: The general planar problem, and triangulated or other planar classes outside grid-covered cylinders.

events.what_happened: Zongqing Chen, Sergey Kitaev and Brian Y. Sun, 'Word-representability of subdivisions of triangular grid graphs', arXiv:1503.08002 (later published as 'Word-representability of face subdivisions of triangular grid graphs', Graphs and Combinatorics, 2016, per a search snippet). Characterises word-representable subdivisions (face subdivisions, which replace some cells of a triangular grid graph by plane copies of K4) using 'smart orientations', a notion introduced there. Corollary: any subdivision of the boundary triangles of the Sierpiński gasket graph is word-representable.

disputes.summary: Glen (2016, arXiv:1605.01688) states that K4-free near-triangulations are word-representable iff 3-colourable. Roy and Hariharasubramanian (2026) say they rectify a result of Glen's paper that they state as 'word-representable iff perfect'. Not resolved from my reading. The cross-pass should compare Glen's theorem statement with the Roy paper's wording.

Kitaev and Sun (2021, published RAIRO 2024) revised the list of non-word-representable graphs on seven vertices (25 listed). Roy and Hariharasubramanian (2026) report a further minimal non-word-representable seven-vertex graph that is not among the 25. Whether the corrected count is now different, and whether the new graph is planar, I did not establish.

summary: Nothing in the sources I read characterises the word-representable planar graphs, and none of the events claims to. The only 2024–2026 result touching the planar characterisation is Roy and Hariharasubramanian (arXiv:2605.25733, posted 25 May 2026). It claims a forbidden-induced-subgraph characterisation of word-representable near-triangulations (planar graphs whose inner faces are all triangles), including those containing K4. This is a proper subclass of planar graphs. The authors' own introduction says word-representability of planar graphs 'remains one of the most challenging problems in this area', so, as a call on this bullet, it is a restricted-class result rather than a resolution. The sources I read give the planar item as open: the Kitaev–Lozin survey lists 'Characterise (non-)word-representable planar graphs' as an open problem (survey text read in the arXiv PDF, which is the 2017 version), and the Wikipedia article on word-representable graphs, read through a summarising fetch that reports a revision date of 9 August 2026, lists the same item and cites no 2024–2026 results. Close calls: (a) the Roy abstract says 'complete characterization of word-representable near-triangulations', and someone who treats near-triangulations as the hard planar case may read more into it; I think the authors' own framing supports the narrower reading. (b) Triangle-free planar graphs and planar graphs with at most 3 triangles are 3-colourable, hence word-representable, so the open part is the triangle-rich planar graphs with non-triangular faces; the Roy result covers some of that but not all. I recorded two doubts about the Roy paper: it corrects two earlier published results (Glen 2016 and Kitaev–Sun 2024/2021) and states Glen's result differently from Glen's own abstract; and its PDF was not readable with my tools, so theorem statements come from an HTML fetch summarised by a small model and I did not read the proofs or the Figure 8 graphs. Older partial results on restricted planar classes (2014–2016: convex polyomino triangulations, a single domino tile, grid-covered cylinder triangulations, face subdivisions, K4-free near-triangulations) are recorded as events with predates_frozen_revision true, as the Roy abstract lists them as earlier work. Neighbouring events that do not bear on the planar question (1-11-representability, the Hefty et al. general open problems, modular decomposition, melon graphs, tensor products of wheels, the Kitaev–Sun non-word-representability tools) are recorded as discounted, with the reason. AI: no source I read connects an AI system to word-representable planar graphs, or to word-representability of any planar class. The Kitaev–Sun computer-generated proofs are produced by the authors' own software, which is not an AI system. Searches for lab announcements, AI-discovered counterexamples and LLM acknowledgements in this area returned nothing relevant. The mid-2026 aggregator reports of AI results (GPT-5.6, Devin, Graffiti conjecture 154, Dinitz–Garg–Goemans, the cycle double cover claim) concern other graph problems and are unverified secondary reports. The AutoGraphForge preprint (arXiv:2609.03478, 3 September 2026) names DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B and OProver-32B as provers for graph conjectures generally, and its abstract makes no claim about word-representability. ai.none_found is true across events because none of the sources names a system with a role here; for the Roy paper, that rests on the abstract page and the summarised HTML, not on a verbatim read of the full text. Sibling item: the Kitaev–Lozin survey lists 'Characterize word-representable near-triangulations (containing K4)' as a separate open item. The Roy result addresses that item, not this one; I have not checked whether Wikipedia's January 2024 list contains the sibling as a separate bullet, which is for the cross-pass to resolve.
competing_reading: The strongest case for reading the record more generously: Roy and Hariharasubramanian claim a complete characterisation of word-representable near-triangulations, including K4-containing ones, and the sources say that planar graphs with few triangles are 3-colourable (hence word-representable). On that view the hard planar cases are triangle-rich planar graphs, which is essentially the near-triangulation setting, so the bullet's substantive content may be substantially settled. Against that reading: the class of planar graphs with at least one non-triangular inner face is outside the paper's theorem, and the authors themselves say the planar problem remains open. The narrower reading (a restricted-class result, bullet still open) is the one the authors' own text supports.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A verbatim read of arXiv:2605.25733 (the PDF was not readable with my tools): Theorem 16's exact scope, the Figure 8 graphs and whether any result goes beyond near-triangulations. (2) A journal acceptance or a referee report on the Roy paper, and any later paper that cites it as settling planar graphs or states the planar problem is still open. (3) A verbatim comparison of Glen's Theorem 2 with the Roy paper's 'iff perfect' statement of it. (4) For the cross-pass: whether the January 2024 Wikipedia list has the sibling item on near-triangulations containing K4 as a separate bullet, since the Roy result answers that item. (5) Whether the Kitaev–Lozin book's wording of the planar item matches the frozen Wikipedia statement, which I have taken as given.
